overview.method: Labeled contact-sheet overview; not full-resolution inspection of every image

groups.title: Softness is not one fixed anatomy
groups.claim: The early pictures include both a plush miniature and freely drawn shapes. The common strength is intimacy, not a single eye size, muzzle length, or technique.
items: A plush-like opening
The small dark eyes, broad pale muzzle, stubby limbs and tactile fur make this read as a little toy. This is evidence for compactness, not for large cartoon eyes.
The actual chapter-three illustration

Mother has a long upright torso and pointed muzzle; the child is a tiny rounded figure beside carrots. Their size contrast and affection matter more here than literal proportions. Neither figure visibly wears boots, despite boots in the text.
A painted oval
The belly and quill halo nearly make one round silhouette, with paws tucked against it. This is a different drawing language from image34, even though both are compact.

groups.title: Animal anatomy remains a real alternative
groups.claim: Naturalistic pictures should not be dismissed as incapable of emotion. They express through posture, proximity and environment, while giving less room to exaggerated facial acting.
items: Low to the ground
The pair has pointed muzzles and low quilled backs; limbs are largely concealed. This is useful animal anatomy, but a group picture is not a reliable individual model sheet.
A miniature with a yellow back
Two small figures share a bowl; one has a striking yellow quilled back. That does not establish a rule that PinPin always has a wholly golden back, or identify which figure is him.
Four-legged during magic
The floating hedgehog has a horizontal torso and four dangling legs. A genuinely animal-shaped body exists even in a magical scene. Upright posture is not universal.

groups.title: The strongest counterexample is inside chapter 16
groups.claim: These are three pictures associated with the same snowy journey, not a child-to-adult timeline. Clothing, hands, feet and proportions change together. My earlier claim that one compact body was the established answer was too strong.
items: Tiny bare paws
The upright oval has almost no neck, very short arms and tiny bare feet. Its large dark eyes and recognizable muzzle make small gestures readable.
Visible legs and shoes
A longer muzzle, coat, scarf, more articulated arms and a visible stepping leg give this PinPin a different silhouette. Brown footwear is already in the original, not just the farm adaptation.
Coat with bare feet
This action pose combines an open coat, a rounded belly, finger-like paws and a long raised bare foot. Clothes do not imply boots, and action does not preserve the other pictures' proportions.

groups.title: Rendering and costume are separate decisions
groups.claim: Calling everything 'storybook' hides important differences. A painterly animal, a dressed dimensional character and a flatter comic figure can share a story without sharing a design system.
items: Saturated expressive painting
The orange pointed face, vivid blue-green forest and long stepping legs differ sharply from the pale rounded figures. The original includes expressive color and visible legs, too.
Tailored clothing, compact body
A waistcoat, sleeves and bow tie sit on a rounded body with bare clawed feet. Because this is a family-context image, I do not assume it is a definitive PinPin portrait.
Large-eyed clothed figure

The large eyes, swept forehead quills, waistcoat and cloak produce a more youthful, humanoid impression. Facial proportions change as well as clothing. Its table hides the feet, so it proves nothing about footwear.

groups.title: The wizard is recognizable, but continuity is not solved
groups.claim: The later green outfit is a strong identity cue. It must not conceal a different face or body each time. The original's family groups also require care about which hedgehog is the protagonist.
items: Clothed family, bare feet
Several plate-carrying hedgehogs have clothes and visible little bare feet. They cannot all be treated as different portraits of PinPin.
Size is relational
The tiny recipient of a leafy hat is surrounded by larger figures. His smallness is communicated through the relationship, not just a numerical body ratio.
The leaf-hatted wizard
The long green cloak and large pointed hat conceal much of the body. Small brown paws appear at the hem. This supports the costume, not a complete underlying anatomy specification.
A different face under the hat
At breakfast, the smiling muzzle and cheeks look fuller than in image32. Same costume family, still variation in the face. The table conceals the lower body.

groups.title: Some apparent variants are not PinPin evidence
groups.claim: Subject identification comes before character design. A mentor, a bird or an uncertain group cannot silently be counted as another version of the hero.
items: A mentor-context figure
Chapter 2 concerns the elder Master Shipostav. Glasses, a hat and a pale beard-like face belong to that context; they are not evidence that PinPin normally wears spectacles.
An owl-like ambiguity

Also in chapter 2, this figure has round glasses, a beard-like face and an owl-like appearance. The prose describes an elder hedgehog, but the image is ambiguous. I would flag the mismatch, not turn it into a PinPin variant.
Setting, not a portrait
The most prominent subject is a black bird beside a chair and table. The picture informs the domestic setting, not PinPin's muzzle or feet.
Another uncertain elder-like figure
The large quilled figure wears a coat and has bare feet, alongside two birds. The chapter's departure scene does not justify confidently treating that large figure as the young hero.

farm: Clear contours and a pale expressive face stay readable under the leaf hat. This is a useful flat-drawing reference; the costume is later-story evidence, not chapter-three clothing.
Visible brown soles and almost no exposed shin sit under the cloak. Two bear figures also appear, so this page should not be copied as a reliable cast-composition model.
Eyes shut, muzzle relaxed, one little paw beside the face: the farm character works in a domestic scene, not only in action. Bedding hides the legs.
The walking panels show brown footwear and a short body beneath the coat. Boots are historical. Their scale and frequency remain design choices.
The little hand holding the wand, open mouth and strong eye direction make a complicated action easy to read. The crop gives little evidence about feet.
PinPin remains much smaller than the bear, including in the full-body harvest panel. Brown boots appear without making long exposed legs the dominant feature.
excluded: Unapproved new chapter-one artwork; not used as historical evidence or generation reference.

repair.prompt: Edit only panel 1 of this five-panel storyboard: remove the single freestanding brown boot lying on the floor BETWEEN the child hedgehog and the mother, near horizontal center. Replace it with the exact continuous rug/floor background. Keep the boot worn on the child's foot and the boot held by Mother, so exactly TWO boots remain. Do not remove or alter either character's paws. Preserve every other pixel as closely as possible: all characters, expressions, anatomy, lighting, color, crop, five panel frames, props, all of panels 2-5. Do not add text. This is a local prop continuity repair, not a restyling. Output the same 1024x1536 portrait composition.

Mother still has sharper, more naturalistic quills than the child. His alert arrival does not clearly convey the prose's fatigue; the tiny face communicates less change until the final closed-eye scenes. The craft effect is stronger on PinPin than on the polished room.

trials.status: Anatomy revision awaiting user review; user likes original G28 style
limitations: The central floor motif is still an invented continuity aid, not source evidence. The room remains grand and polished, and the far end is visible despite the prose's immense distance. The final upright pose and tiny smile are acting choices, not a discovered mystery.

Lilia's ears and tail are still cropped in the opening frames despite the framing instruction. Her face retains more cartoon modeling than PinPin's. At the end the candle rests on a rock instead of remaining airborne; the quieter faces also give limited evidence of surprise changing to trust.

PinPin's darker quill cap is not a reliable identifier in every panel, and the plush shapes still blur family identity. Mother's final touch reads near his cheek rather than distinctly at his ear. Toy animals added to the shelves are new props, not original story evidence. The quills remain more sharp and polished than the source plush.
